title: Celtics-Sixers Is Can’t-Miss Theater. Here’s What I’m Looking For.
contentHtml:
By the time you read this, I may already be on the Amtrak to Philadelphia. I could not miss the first Celtics-Sixers game since the earthquake of the Jaylen Brown trade.

I love this decades-old rivalry. It hasn’t quite gotten its due because there has been minimal peak crossover between these teams since the 1980s. It’s not Celtics-Lakers, but it should be almost that exalted in historical terms.

It was the other defining rivalry of the 1960s—Wilt Chamberlain against Bill Russell, two dominant centers almost as different in on-court style and substance as the two cities they represented. The best book about it—and one of my favorite basketball books ever—is literally called The Rivalry, by John Taylor. There are dozens of books about the 1980s Celtics, most of which touch on the rivalry in that era—including their classic seven-game series in 1981—and Luke Epplin’s recent book, Moses and the Doctor, gives the 1980s Sixers the spotlight.

The Sixers finally got one over on Boston last season, rallying from 3-1 down behind a reinvigorated Joel Embiid, doing the once impossible and winning Game 7 in Boston, and sending the Celtics into an existential crisis that ended, somehow, with Brown in Philly and Paul George in Boston. What a juicy what-if that series is. If Boston had won Game 7, would Brown still be a Celtic? Or would the Knicks, on an all-time heater, have incinerated the Celtics in the second round as they did the Sixers—and had Boston scurrying to revamp its roster? For that matter, what if the Sixers had won a game or two against the Knicks in the second round?

No matter now. Brown is a Sixer. The bitter tension surrounding his trade hovers over Boston’s entire season and drives the hype for this first clash between Brown and Jayson Tatum—the star who was kept.

All the noise—food metaphors and beyond—surrounding the Brown-Tatum pseudo-feud is a little sad given all they accomplished together, including winning the 2024 title. Brian Scalabrine, Boston’s TV analyst, created a bit of a kerfuffle by claiming Brown requested a trade—only for Brown and his representatives to deny that, and Scalabrine to walk back his report.

I’m not sure it matters what, exactly, went down. Something clearly changed within the team in Tatum’s absence last season. Brown labeled it his favorite season ever, a remark he had to know would cause a stir—triply so because it came hours after Philly eliminated Boston in a series in which Brown underperformed.

A player doesn’t have to explicitly demand a trade in order for everyone involved to understand a change might be necessary. Marc Spears has reported on ESPN twice now that the Celtics “favored” Tatum, even pointing out that the team reinserted Tatum into the coveted anchor spot in starting lineup introductions once Tatum returned from injury last season.

Brown over the weekend reiterated that he and Tatum haven’t talked recently and that they have “nothing to talk about.” When a video was released on Instagram revealing Tatum’s shock at hearing Brown had been dealt to Philly, Brown chimed in with the “cap” emoji in a comment—indicating he thought Tatum’s surprise was not totally genuine. He then declined to explain what the emoji meant, needless evasion when everyone knew.

For the Celtics brass, there was no way to separate any internal tension from the realities of roster building. Brown is 30, due $185 million over the next three seasons. The Celtics flipped him for George, who is much older—36—but due $111 million over two seasons. More pertinent: Brown will be eligible for a mega-extension in July and is at the age where he will want one—if not for the maximum salary, then for something close to it. (He was already eligible for an extension as a Celtic last summer, but under league rules, the trade to Philly pushed the trigger date back a year.) The Celtics may not feel any pressure to even re-sign George once his deal is up. If anything was off-kilter internally, this past summer was the time for Boston to deal. The risk was trading some present-day championship equity for more in the future.

For the Celtics, judging the Brown deal was always going to be at least in part about the Move After the Move—what Brad Stevens and Co. do with the salary wiggle room and extra draft picks the Brown trade netted. In the meantime, they wagered that George would fit well, Tatum would recover in full from an Achilles tear, and the team would win a ton of regular-season games—at least positioning them to do damage in the playoffs.

As their first game against each other approaches on Tuesday night, both teams have been proved right to some degree. It’s early, but Boston and Philly are a combined 17-4, sitting in the top two spots in the East standings. George is averaging 20 points and draining almost 43 percent of his 3s. His penchant for deflections has helped turn a chronically conservative defense into a turnover-forcing machine. Boston has also vaulted from the basement to around league average in free throw rate and shot attempts within the restricted area. They promised to evolve from being Team Extreme—all 3s, no turnovers on either end—and they have.

Brown is averaging 22 points per game and shooting well, and though he is not as central to Philly as he was to Boston in his self-proclaimed favorite season, he is finding his spots even within Philly’s loaded starting five—mashing mismatches, racing up the floor in transition, shooting more corner 3s, sneaking inside on quick cuts.

Brown is in his prime and durable, and he, Tyrese Maxey, and VJ Edgecombe should help Philly maintain a pretty high floor during those inevitable periods when LeBron shows his age and Embiid’s knees flare up. Heck, Embiid is laboring now, and Philly is 9-2.
